_source.displaydescription:
The Cilancva area is the highest point in Kirtipur, located in its eastern part. A huge Cilancva Caitya (KIR0001) stands at the centre of the site. There are numerous other Buddhist monuments in the Caitya premises, which is collectively known as Cilancva Bāhāḥ, a major Buddhist monastery in Kirtipur. It is also called Jagatapāla Mahāvihāra, Mū Bāhāḥ, Gũ Vihāra, Padmakāṣṭhagīri Vihāra, and Kipū Bāhāḥ etc.

Kirtipur was under the Patan rule during the medieval period. Thus, Cilancva Bāhāḥ is listed as one of the Mahāvihāras of Patan. The Nepālikabhūpavaṃśāvalī (19.3.26) also mentions that King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla listed this Bāhāḥ as one of the fifteen Mahāvihāras maintained by Patan. The members of this Bāhāḥ still part take in the Buddhist rituals and festivals held in Patan such as the Samyak Festival and other seasonal processions.

Majority of the scholars conclude that this Bāhāḥ was constructed by Jagata Varmā, a Mahāpātra of Patan, almost at the same time when he constructed Cilancva Caitya (KIR0001) in 1515 CE. However, the inscription recording the construction of this Caitya does not explicitly mention Cilancva Bāhāḥ, but refers to this area as 'Padmakāṣṭhagīri which resembles the heaven (padmakāṣṭhagīri bhanne nāmale svargajastai suhāiraheko ṭhāũ). It indicates that Jagata Pāla could have established a Bāhāḥ called Padmakāṣṭhagīri in the Cilancva premises which was later known as Cilancva Bāhāḥ.[1]He also renovated Bāghabhairava Mandira (KIR0004) in 1571 CE (NS 635). Since his wife Rūpalakṣmī (cf. D. Vajrācārya VS 2056, 478) was from Kirtipur (Locke 1985, 180), she could have encouraged him to construct and renovate these highly significant monuments.

The southern entrance to Cilancva Caitya and the main entrance to Cilancva Bāhāḥ’s dyaḥchẽ are parallel to each other, revealing the architectural similarity of both monuments. A pair of lions installed in 1716 CE (NS 836) flanks the dyaḥchẽ’s main entrance. Similarly, two metal statues (Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana) are placed to the right and to the left of the entrance respectively, which is a common feature of the bāhāḥs. A carved wooden toraṇa also crowns the entrance. Right above the toraṇa, a pasukājhyāḥ can be seen on the dyaḥchẽ’s first floor. In addition to the main entrance, the dyaḥchẽ has two additional doors in its façade. Two trikhājhyāḥs are also installed on the dyaḥchẽ’s first floor, right above these additional doors. The wooden toraṇa above the main entrance was stolen sometime ago, thus the toraṇa, crowning the eastern door, was shifted here.  

The toraṇas, kept above its eastern door, were removed during the renovation of the dyaḥchẽ building in 2015 CE. A statue of Cakrasamvara is concentrated as the āgaṃdyaḥ on the dyaḥchẽ’s first floor. Until a few decades ago, one could see some traditional wall paintings on the first floor. They were completely destroyed during the renovation of the building (cf. Ś. Śreṣṭha VS 2057, 67). The first floor is now empty and used by the members of the saṅgha for organising the community feasts, lectures, seminars etc. There is a balcony on the façade of this floor. The roof of the dyaḥchẽ is tiled with jhĩgaṭī and a pura crowned by three pinnacles is installed on its top.  

Locke (1985, 180) mentions the beams, which support the aforementioned balcony, bearing the inscriptions from 1629 CE (NS 749) and 1680 CE (NS 800). They suggest that the Bāhāḥ must have been renovated in those dates. A local resident named Candramāna Vajrācārya repaired the roof in around 1889 CE after it was destroyed by a wind (Ś. Śreṣṭha VS 2057, 68). The latest renovation of the dyaḥchẽ was carried out by the Department of Archaeology after it was destroyed during the 2015 CE earthquakes.

Cilancva Bāhāḥ has a saṅgha consisting of the members from the Śākya and Vajrācārya clans. Each Vajrācārya member is responsible to carry out the daily worship for two weeks. The ritual worship is followed by a traditional music, gambāḥsĩ, which is a unique feature of the major bāhāḥs of Patan. The anniversary worship of the Bāhāḥ is held on the full moon day of Asoja. The statue of Cakrasamvara, concerted inside the āgaṃ, is worshiped by the Pradhāna caste community members of Kirtipur on the dark moon day of Vaiśākha (the Mātātīrtha Aũśī day) as their clan deity.

The Bāhāḥ had a guṭhī consisting of six ropānīs of land for each elder member (thakālī) of the saṅgha for performing the daily and annual rituals. In addition to this, the guṭhī had a pond and flower garden. However, the mentioned guṭhī property cannot be traced out in present-day. The Bāhāḥ had a huge collection of metal statues dating from the seventh and eighth centuries. Because of a dispute that arose amongst the saṅgha members in around 1980 CE, the statues were handed over to the Guṭhī Saṃsthāna and National Museum (cf. Ś. Śreṣṭha VS 2057, 68-69).

Footnotes

  1. ^ This Bāhāḥ is referred to as ‘Padmakāṣṭhagīri Gũ Vihāra concerted according to the customs’ in the invitation letter sent from Paśupati Bāhāḥ to the member of Cilancva Bāhāḥ in 1574 (NS 694) requesting them to participate to the Samyak festival (cf. Vajrācārya VS 2061, 117). Since the invitation letter does not refer to the Bāhāḥ as consecrated by Jagatapāla, one may cast doubt on whether he was its initial constructor.

Yāka Bāhāḥ is located on the northwestern part of the Cilancva Caitya premises (KIR0001) and is one of the branches (kacā) of Cilancva Mahāvihāra (KIR0002). The Bāhāḥ is also called Jīvadharma Mahāvihāra (see the inscription from NS 801 below), and its courtyard can be entered through an astonishingly carved wooden door. A set of artistically carved trikhā windows can be seen above this door. The Bāhāḥ’s dyaḥchẽ (house for the Bāhāḥ’s primary deity) is built in the courtyard, facing east. A stone statue of Akṣobhya is enshrined as the Bāhāḥ’s kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ (primary deity) inside the sanctum, which is located on the dayaḥchẽ’s ground floor. Besides the kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ, there were several other small Buddhist statues and caityas inside the sanctum, however, they were stolen in the course of time. A pair of lions and elephants (established in 1710 CE, i.e., 830 NS) are installed on either side of the entrance to the sanctum. The entrance is adorned with traditional carvings but has no toraṇa above it. The dyaḥchẽ’s first floor has a set of pasukā windows, and its roof is covered with corrugated pewter sheets (jastāpātā).

The inscription dating 1680 CE (801 NS) installed in the Bāhāḥ premises attests that Yākaḥ Bāhāḥ was constructed in 1647 CE (767 NS) by the Rathasyana Vajrācārya, his son Jīvarāja, and other family members. It also mentions that King Siddhinarasiṃha Malla, too, was present during the inaugural ceremony of the Bāhāḥ. Jīvarāja, the main founder of the Bāhāḥ, died sixteen years after its completion. Several statues of Buddha, as well as, Lokeśvara, Prajñāpāramitā, Gaṇeśa, and Mahākāla statues were installed in the Bāhāḥ premises in the memory of Jivarāja by his family members. On the same date, his two sons also endowed four and a half ropanīs of land and established a guṭhī to sponsor the Bāhāḥ’s anniversary rituals. The other inscriptions (see below) installed in the Bāhāḥ suggest that a number of statues and architectural artifacts were installed here in the late medieval period.

In 1970s, the statue of Cakrasamvara and other metal statues enshrined inside the āgaṃ (the shrine on the dyaḥchẽ’s first floor built for the Bāhāḥ’s esoteric deities and rituals), were also stolen. Due to the lack of regular maintenance, the roof of the dyaḥchẽ collapsed in 2009 CE, and covered the kvāḥpāḥdyaḥ. In 2011CE, some residents of the region restored the roof, covering it with corrugated pewter sheets (jastāpātā) funded by the local government. The building which has the main entrance to the Bāhāḥ’s courtyard was damaged during the 2015 CE earthquakes. Due to a dispute over its ownership, no one has renovated it since then.

Although the inscription (see below) offers a detailed account of the traditions of daily worship, annual rituals, lighting up oil lamp on the full moon day of Kārtika, and so forth to be performed in the Bāhāḥ, no one carries out these rituals in the present-day. Until two decades ago, a Vajrācārya caste member used to perform the daily worship and annual rituals in the Bāhāḥ. Unfortunately, no one took over these tasks after he died. There is no one left who is directly related to this Bāhāḥ, thus it is slowly falling into oblivion.
_source.displayname: Yākaḥ Bāhāḥ (built in 1647 CE) || याक: बाहा: ।। KIR0020

I Bāhāḥ is located approximately 50 metres south of Ikhālakhu Square on the way to Tabāhāl, and lies on the right-hand side of the street. The Bāhāḥ can be accessed through an opening on a boundary wall to the east. It has been heavily reconstructed and was converted to a four-storey residential building after the 2015 earthquakes. The original architecture of the building has been completely destroyed, so that only traces of the brass-clad door, two blind windows and some layers of cornices remain today (in 2019). The main building is raised on a plinth which is 60 cm high. At the centre of the stone-paved courtyard one can find a vajradhātu caitya and a dharmādhātu maṇḍala. The courtyard is surrounded by residential buildings on three of the four cardinal directions, with the eastern side as the exception. The courtyard has two alleyways that lead out to the smaller courtyards; these can be found to its west and its south. 

The Bāhāḥ is a private vihāra constructed by a Joshi family; it is not a branch of any larger bāhāḥ. Images of lions sitting on elephants can be found on either side of the main entrance, and small carved windows adorn the wall here. Upon entering the sanctum, one immediately sees an image of Akṣobhya facing to the east. Two brass statues of Yama holding kāladaṇḍa (the staff of death) and pāśa (a noose) are also housed in the sanctum, with one on either side of the main door. An empty triangular niche to the left of the door is worshipped as  Hanumān.

Accoding to Pruscha (1975, 133), this vihāra was constructed in the 16th century.

According to Locke (1985, 140) two metal flags used to flank the door and a toraṇa was installed above the main entrance. This contained an image of Akṣobhya. However, it seems that the toraṇa was removed by the residing family of the vihāra some time around 2008. Moreover, Locke states that a trikhā jhyāla (triple window) and a bāku jhyāla (lit. halved window) can be found in the façade of the first floor.  The building was severely damaged and was no longer safe to live in. Therefore the owner demolished the building and reconstructed it in a modern style. After the reconstruction the family sold the building. Local people say that the family also sold the ground floor of the building where the kvāpādyaḥ of the vihāra is enshrined. 

The bell was donated in VS 1959.

Thapāḥ Bahī is a branch of Guji Bāhāḥ and is located at Thapāḥ Ṭola near to Thapāḥ Hiṭī. A series of steps to the north of the Bahī lead up to its courtyard. There is no gate at the courtyard's entrance, which is unusual for this kind of monument. The god house of this Bahī is very simple, and lacks both a toraṇa above the door as well as the stone lions one usually finds in front of such a structure.

A historical photo of the Bahī printed in Pruscha (1975, 196) shows that the god house once had a tiled roof with dormer (bhaipvāḥ) on top. However, later photos published in Locke (1985, 198) show CGI sheets covering the roof, and indeed this is still the case. The first floor of the god house has a simple lattice window on its façade and an āgamachẽ inside it. The ground floor of the house contains a sanctum with a stone image of an east-facing Akṣobhya. The statue's body is covered with metal cloth (hẽgā). A miniature image of this larger one can be found next to it. The god house was badly damaged by the 2015 earthquake and is now supported by wooden columns.

A Phalcā containing an image of Mahākāla sits on the northern side of the courtyard. Meanwhile, an Aśoka Caitya marks the centre of the courtyard.

Vasu Bāhāḥ is a branch of Rudravarṇa Mahāvihāra, Oku Bāhāḥ (LAL2260). Unlike other bāhāḥs in Patan and elsewhere, this Bāhāḥ does not have a proper shrine (kvāḥpāḥchẽ) for the Bāhāḥ’s primary deity (kvāpāḥdyaḥ). Instead of a kvāḥpāḥchẽ, a small temple is built in the Bāhāḥ’s courtyard (called kvāḥpāḥdegaḥ), and a statue of Akṣobhya is enshrined inside its sanctum. The temple is plastered with cement and capped by a caitya as its pinnacle.  A stone toraṇa on which the images of Five Buddhas (Pañcabuddha) have been carved, is installed above the entrance to the sanctum.  

An additional stone statue of Akṣobhya which is slightly bigger than the main one is installed behind the main statue of Akṣobhya in the sanctum. Majāḥdegaḥ is a caitya standing on a steep slope to the south of the Cilancva Bāhāḥ (KIR0001). It is built atop four-layered stone plinth. Unlike many other caityas in Kirtipur, the plinths of Majāḥdegaḥ are larger in size. Its topmost plinth is entirely made of stones.

The local residents believe that these plinths must have been raised to build a temple,however no temple was ever built. For this reason, they refer to it as Majāḥdegaḥ, meaning incomplete temple. However, there is no evidence to verify these assumptions.

Images of Tārā and Buddha are carved on four cardinal directions of the caitya, in accordance with the traditions. Besides these images, some smaller icons of other deities (similar to the ones carved on Yatālibi Caitya (LAL2250) and found in Micchu Bāhāḥ (LAL1100)) are also carved on it (cf. Ś. Śreṣṭha VS 2057, 64). Above these statues, a dome, harmikā, thirteen bhuvanas, and āmalaka motifs are carved.

There is no evidence to date the initial construction of this monument. However, the motifs carved on the caitya suggest that it was perhaps built sometime between seventeenth and eighteenth century.

It is probable that someone from the Vajrācārya castes living around this caitya might have constructed it. In 1990s, an iron sheet was welded around this caitya for its protection (Shokoohy and others 2014, 313). The Kirtipur Municipality renovated its plinths in 2010 CE.

There is no guṭhī associated to this caitya. Even the elders of the area cannot recall any religious, social, or cultural activity (other than Bāhāḥ Cāḥ Hilegu) that used to be organised here.

Kusi Bāhāḥ is one of the branches (kacā) of the Cilancva Bāhāḥ (KIR0002), located at Kusicā, to the southwest of the Cilancva Bāhāḥ premises. Kusi Bāhāḥ is also known by its Sanskrit name, Mahendrakīrti Vihāra, and (cf. Ś. Śreṣṭha VS 2057, 69). Locke (1985, 182) mention it as Mahākīrti Vihāra.

The bāhāḥ is accessible after walking down a flight of fifteen staircases through the ground floor of a private residential building. From the outside of this building, it is hard to assume that there is a bāhāḥ behind it. This could be the reason why Karl Pruscha was not able to locate and include this bāhāḥ in his inventory (published in 1975 CE).  

The bāhāḥ has a rectangular courtyard and its dyaḥchẽ (main shrine) faces northeast. The door of the dyaḥchẽ is intricately carved, however, it lacks a toraṇa. Instead of a toraṇa, an image of Vajrasattva is carved on the door’s upper part. A stone statue of Akṣobhya is consecrated as the kvāpādyaḥ (bāhāḥ’s primary deity) inside the dyaḥchẽ’s sanctum. There used to be a mural on the wall inside the sanctum, however, it is completely destroyed.

The dyaḥchẽ has a pasukājhyāḥ (traditional wooden window) and an āgaṃ (shrine for the bāhāḥ’s esoteric deity) on its first floor. Cakrasaṃvara is consecrated in the āgaṃ (based on a personal conversation with a local resident, from a Vajrācārya caste, male, age 56). Originally, the roof of the dyaḥchẽ was tiled with jhĩgaṭī. After it started leaking, the responsible Vajrācārya clan replaced it with corrugated pewter sheets in 2001 CE. A Śikharakūṭa Caitya is established in the middle of the bāhāḥ courtyard.

There is no evidence to date the bāhāḥ’s initial construction. The wood carving on the dyaḥchẽ can be dated from the seventeenth and eighteenth century.

A Vajrācārya family, residing in front of the bāhāḥ, are members of the saṅgha of the Cilancva Bāhāḥ, and responsible for maintaining the Bāhāḥ and carrying out the daily and other rituals. They believe that one of their ancestors constructed it.

Two Śākya families, who are not members of the saṅgha of the Cilancva Bāhāḥ, perform their initiation (bare chuigu) ceremonies here. These families moved to Kirtipur some generations back and the Vajrācāryas of the Cilancva Bāhāḥ gave them the permission to use Kusi Bāhāḥ for their initiation ceremonies (cf. Locke 1985, 182).

Every year, on the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, the main gate of the bāhāḥ is open for twenty-four hours to allow the local community members to worship the kvāpādyaḥ. On other days, the main gate and the sanctum entrance are kept locked.

Yākaḥ Phalcā is located to the south of Gaṇeśa Mandira (LAL0157) in Om Bāhāḥ Ṭola. The Phalcā is open to the north and west, with just one bay on each side. A single-bayed structure is called yākaḥ in Newari and the Phalcā is named accordingly. The Phalcā has three carved columns and six struts. The roof is sloping down to the northern and western sides. There is an empty niche on the eastern wall of the Phalcā. According to local residents, the previous Phalcā building had a niche on the same the wall of the same direction and there were statues of Nārāyaṇa and Umāmaheśvara in the niches, which were lost before some decades. A small Gaṇeśa shrine stands next to Yākaḥ Phalcā, towards the south. It is still worshipped.  

No historical record is available to date the Phalcā. However, according to the local Śreṣṭha community made it around 250 years before. In the 1934 earthquakes, the building collapsed. It was then reconstructed (n.d.). In 1989, local residents demolished the crumbling structure and in 2019, the Lalitpur Municipality reconstructed it with the help of seven lakh Nepali rupees. An electric power pole stands behind the Phalcā and quasi-encroached the building. Every year on the 11th day of the bright fortnight of the Bhādra, an image of Yamāḥdyaḥ (Indra) is exhibited on top of an erected pole and on the 13th day, samaybaji (a ritual snack) is distributed. On the 4th day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina, the images are taken down. In earlier times, similar six images of Yamāḥdyaḥ were exhibited.
